def: Rules that decide who can use which systems and data, and what they can do with them.
Microsoft's directory service that manages users, computers and permissions in most company networks. A top target for attackers.
A well-resourced group, often state-backed, that breaks in and stays hidden for a long time to spy or steal.
Software that shows unwanted ads, sometimes bundled with free downloads.
Testing an AI system with permission by trying to make it misbehave, leak data or ignore its rules.
Software that detects and removes known malware. Modern tools add behavior monitoring (see EDR).
Application Programming Interface: a defined way for programs to talk to each other. APIs need authentication and input checks like any web page.
Address Resolution Protocol: how a device on a local network finds the hardware (MAC) address that belongs to an IP address. Attackers abuse it to sweep or spoof a network.
A list of every device, account and piece of software an organization has. You cannot protect what you do not know about.
All the places an attacker could try to get in: internet-facing services, accounts, devices, people and suppliers.
Proving who you are, for example with a password, a passkey or a fingerprint.
Deciding what an authenticated person is allowed to do.
A hidden way into a system that bypasses normal security, left by an attacker or, rarely, a developer.
A copy of data kept so it can be restored after loss or ransomware. Keep at least one copy offline or immutable.
An encoding that writes any data with 64 safe characters. Anyone can decode it, so it hides nothing.
Defenders who protect, monitor and respond. Opposite of the red team.
Many infected devices controlled together by an attacker, often used for spam or DDoS attacks.
Guessing a password or key by trying many possibilities, often automatically.
A program where organizations pay researchers who responsibly report vulnerabilities.
A security competition where you solve challenges to find hidden "flags".
Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three goals of security.
Data sent or stored without encryption, readable by anyone who sees it. FTP and Telnet send passwords in cleartext.
Protecting data, identities and workloads hosted by cloud providers such as AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
The channel malware uses to receive instructions from an attacker.
A bug where user input ends up inside an operating system command, letting an attacker run their own commands.
Meeting the security rules required by laws, contracts or standards, such as HIPAA, PCI DSS or FERPA.
Stopping an incident from spreading, for example by isolating a device or disabling an account.
Trying usernames and passwords leaked from one site on other sites, betting that people reuse passwords.
A web flaw that lets an attacker run their script in other users' browsers on a trusted site.
The science of protecting information with math: encryption, hashing and digital signatures.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public ID for a known vulnerability, like CVE-2021-44228.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is.
Common Weakness Enumeration: a numbered catalog of software weakness types, like CWE-89 for SQL injection. CVEs are specific bugs; CWEs are the kind of mistake.
Parts of the internet reachable only through special software such as Tor, where stolen data is often traded.
An incident where information is accessed or taken by someone not allowed to have it.
Distributed denial of service: flooding a service with traffic from many devices so real users cannot reach it.
Layering several protections so one failure does not lead to a breach.
Writing, testing and tuning the rules that turn logs into security alerts.
Collecting and analyzing digital evidence in a way that holds up to scrutiny.
DomainKeys Identified Mail: a signature that proves an email came from the domain it claims and was not altered.
An email policy that checks SPF and DKIM line up with the visible From domain, and says what to do if they do not.
Domain Name System: turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
Hiding data or commands inside DNS queries and answers to sneak them past firewalls. Long, random-looking subdomains are a sign.
Endpoint Detection and Response: tools on laptops and servers that record behavior, detect threats and can isolate devices.
Changing how data is written (Base64, hex, URL encoding) so systems can carry it. Unlike encryption, it needs no key to reverse.
Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
Any device people use or that connects to a network: laptops, phones, servers.
Stealing data by moving it out of an organization.
Code or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability.
An alert that fired on harmless activity.
A control that allows or blocks network traffic based on rules.
Low-level software built into hardware, such as a computer's UEFI.
Governance, risk and compliance: the policy and risk side of security.
Passwords or keys written directly into code or config files. Anyone who sees the repo gets them.
Turning data into a fixed-length fingerprint that cannot be reversed. Used to check integrity and store passwords.
A decoy system set up to attract and study attackers.
Identity and Access Management: the systems and rules for accounts and permissions.
Industrial control systems that run physical processes like water treatment and power.
Insecure direct object reference: changing an ID in a request (like invoice 1001 to 1002) shows someone else's data because the app never checks ownership.
The organized way to handle a security incident: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn.
Evidence that a system may be compromised, such as a malicious IP address, domain or file hash.
Rebuilding objects from untrusted data in formats that can run code while loading, which can give an attacker code execution.
Risk from people inside an organization, through malice or mistakes.
A number that identifies a device interface on a network.
A prompt designed to get an AI model past its safety rules.
JSON Web Token: a signed token apps use to say who you are. If the server does not verify the signature, anyone can forge one.
CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog: vulnerabilities attackers are actually using. Patch these first.
Malware that records what you type.
How attackers move from the first compromised machine to others in a network.
Giving people and programs only the access they need, nothing more.
A family of open-source operating systems that runs most servers, cloud systems and security tools.
A record of events, such as logins or errors, written by a system. The raw material of detection.
Malicious software: viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, spyware and more.
An attacker secretly relaying or changing communication between two parties.
Multi-factor authentication: needing two or more kinds of proof to log in, such as a password and a code.
A public knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques.
The US framework that describes cybersecurity work roles, tasks and skills.
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
A link on a trusted site that forwards visitors to any address in a parameter, which phishers use to borrow the site's reputation.
Open-source intelligence: information gathered from public sources.
A widely used list of the most critical web application security risks.
A recording of network traffic, packet by packet, opened in tools like Wireshark to see exactly what crossed the wire.
A passwordless login based on public-key cryptography, resistant to phishing.
An app that creates and stores a unique strong password for every account.
Trying one or two common passwords against many accounts, to stay under lockout limits. The opposite of brute-forcing one account.
An update that fixes bugs, including security vulnerabilities.
Using ../ in a file name to escape the folder an app meant to serve, reaching files like /etc/passwd.
The part of an attack that does the damage, such as the malware delivered by an exploit.
Authorized simulated attacks to find weaknesses before criminals do.
Anything an attacker sets up to keep access after a reboot or password reset, such as a new account or scheduled task.
Fake messages that trick people into clicking, sharing credentials or paying.
A numbered endpoint for network services on a device, such as 443 for HTTPS.
Probing a host for open ports to see which services it runs. Nmap is the classic tool.
Gaining more permissions than you were given, for example from user to admin.
Inputs that make an AI model ignore its instructions, directly or hidden in content it reads.
Red and blue teams working together to improve detection.
Malware that encrypts files and demands payment, often after stealing data.
The first phase of an attack: learning about the target.
Authorized attackers who test an organization's defenses.
The chance something bad happens multiplied by how bad it would be.
Malware that hides deep in the system to avoid detection.
A device that forwards traffic between networks.
An isolated environment for running untrusted code safely.
A firmware feature that only starts software signed by trusted keys.
CompTIA's widely recognized entry-level security certification.
Splitting a network into zones so a breach in one cannot easily reach the others.
Security Information and Event Management: collects logs from everywhere so analysts can search and alert on them.
An open format for writing detection rules that can be converted for many SIEMs.
Security Operations Center: the team that monitors and responds to threats.
Manipulating people instead of computers to gain access or information.
Sender Policy Framework: lists which mail servers may send email for a domain.
Malware that secretly watches what you do.
A flaw where input changes a database query. Prevented with parameterized queries.
A range of IP addresses that forms one network, written like 192.168.1.0/24.
Breaking into a target through a trusted supplier, update or software dependency.
The two main transport protocols. TCP is reliable and connection-based; UDP is fast and connectionless.
The person or group behind an attack.
Proactively searching for attackers who have slipped past existing alerts.
Information about attackers and their methods that helps defenders prepare.
Transport Layer Security: the encryption behind HTTPS.
Software that routes traffic through several relays to hide where it came from.
Malware disguised as something useful.
MFA with exactly two factors.
The modern firmware that starts a computer before the operating system.
A header in each web request that names the client software. Attack tools often reveal themselves in it, though it is easy to fake.
Virtual private network: an encrypted tunnel between a device and a network.
A weakness that could be exploited.
A tool that checks systems for known weaknesses.
Web application firewall: filters malicious web traffic in front of an application.
The free, open-source tool for capturing and inspecting network packets.
Malware that spreads by itself from machine to machine.
A bit operation used in encryption. With a short, reused key it is easy to break, so malware uses it to hide strings, not to protect them.
A vulnerability the vendor does not know about or has not fixed yet.
A model where no user or device is trusted by default, even inside the network; every request is verified.
